newsitem.title: ZAIRE: ZAIRE CAPITAL HUMS WITH PEACE TALK.
newsitem.headline: ZAIRE CAPITAL HUMS WITH PEACE TALK.

text.p: The prospect of talks between Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko and his rebel foe Laurent Kabila has raised hopes in Kinshasa's teeming suburbs that chaos can be averted.

Many inhabitants of the Zairean capital fear that should Mobutu and his allies refuse to go honourably, the remains of his defeated army could bring chaos and carnage to Kinshasa in a final act of desperation as rebels advanced.

"We are not worried about the (rebel) Alliance entering Kinshasa. We are worried about what the army deserters, and all those who may fear they will be chased and judged, will do when they arrive," Mukendi wa Mulumba, an adviser to opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi, told Reuters.
"We are happy that the Americans have launched this dialogue that could bring an end to the conflict," he said, and repeated opposition demands to be included in the negotiating process.
"We hope this means of negotiations will be pursued not only to stop the conflict but also to solve the political crisis. That is not possible without the radical opposition," he said.

Latest reports reaching Kinshasa placed the rebels within about 300 km (200 miles). Demoralised government forces have abandoned more than three-quarters of the vast country. Few Zaireans now believe the army can withstand the rebels' final thrust.
But should Mobutu and his allies choose to stay to the bitter end, their final card could be a "night of the long knives" in which diehard soldiers wreaked havoc, one banker suggested.
After enduring months of rumour and growing insecurity, most Kinshasa inhabitants hope the talks will result in the end of Mobutu's three-decade rule, sparing the capital a fight to the finish.

"We do not want a military victory. That will inflate Mr Kabila's ego even more. He has already achieved enough," sculptor Jean-Pierre Nduwa said. "We would like a diplomatic victory with Mobutu's resignation as the point of departure."
A more radical group of inhabitants gathered in the working class Matonge neighbourhood said negotiations or no negotiations, Mobutu's rule was coming to an end.

Smelling Mobutu's impending demise, radical street activists of the unarmed opposition known after their daily meetings on street corners as "standing parliamentarians" said they would soon be "sitting parliamentarians".
"We are not concerned whether Kabila comes in with force or not. It is Mobutu's people and all those who have stolen with him who have something to fear," one said.

Mobutu agreed after long meetings with U.S. troubleshooter Bill Richardson to what would be the first face-to-face talks with Kabila since the guerrilla leader launched a rebellion in the east of the country last October.
The talks will be hosted by the United Nations and African leaders on a South African navy vessel off the Atlantic coast.
Kabila has consistently said he expects Mobutu to surrender power at the meeting. But the presidential entourage hopes the talks will lead to a transitional arrangement and non-exclusive elections.
